paper.title: The impact of childhood health shocks on parental labor supply
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed. The acknowledgement footnote states: …

registers.name_in_paper: DanDiabKids (the clinical register / Danish registry of childhood and adolescent diabetes)
population registries within Statistics Denmark (the population registry)
variables_mentioned: number of children in the household

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark (labor income, full-time/part-time status, private versus public sector, educational attainment, social assistance)
prescription drug expenditures related to drugs targeting the nervous system (ATC main group N)
variables_mentioned: yearly total spending (copayment + insurance) on ATC main group N drugs
number of pills picked up from pharmacies

linkages: Through population registries within Statistics Denmark, the children can be linked to their parents (child-parent links are possible through the population registry)

Each child with T1D is matched to five control children on exact date of birth and sex; each control child is assigned a pseudo date of diagnosis equal to the actual diagnosis date of the T1D child it serves as control for

sample.universe: Children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in Denmark between 1990 and 2017, observed in DanDiabKids, and their matched control children; and the parents of these children
sample.unit_of_observation: parent-year (a yearly panel from five years before to ten years after the (pseudo-)date of diagnosis)
selection_rules: Children diagnosed with T1D 1990-2017 observed in DanDiabKids (5,838 children)
Each T1D child matched to five control children who do not develop diabetes in the period of observation, matched on exact date of birth and sex (29,190 control children)
Each control child assigned a pseudo date of diagnosis equal to the diagnosis date of its matched T1D child

Children linked to mothers and fathers through the population registry; mothers identified for 5,779 (99%) of the T1D children and 28,671 (98.2%) of the control children; fathers for 5,427 (92.3%) and 26,681 (91.4%)
Yearly panel constructed from five years before onset to ten years after; for diagnoses after 2007 fewer than ten post-diagnosis years are observed because the panel ends in 2017
Log wage income, part-time status and sector are measured conditional on employment / positive wage income
sample.n_observations: up to 478,425 mother-year observations and 442,152 father-year observations in the difference-in-differences regressions of Table 3
sample.n_individuals: 5,838 children diagnosed with T1D and 29,190 matched control children; 5,779 + 28,671 mothers and 5,427 + 26,681 fathers identified

construction_notes: The mean age at T1D onset is 9.34 years (SD 4.05)
Table 1 measures parental characteristics two years prior to the diagnosis year (or the pseudo-date of diagnosis for controls) so that they cannot be impacted by the diagnosis
Log wage income is defined only for parent-years with positive wage income; part-time status and public-sector status are measured conditional on being employed
Prescription drug expenditure aggregates yearly total spending (copayment + insurance) on ATC main group N

Background controls in the difference-in-differences regressions: age, # children, immigrant status, academic education, unskilled worker, parents are living together; the event-study figures adjust for age, # children and parents living together
Standard errors are clustered at the birth cohort by sex matched group level
In Table 4 the year of diagnosis is left out of the analysis to examine longer term impacts, and immigrant status is not controlled for in the panel that tests for differences by immigrant status

claims.statement: Having a child diagnosed with type 1 diabetes changes wage income > 0 (0/1) for mothers in the post-diagnosis period.

treatment.label: DiabetesXPost - child diagnosed with type 1 diabetes (T1D), in the post-diagnosis period

register_source.value: DanDiabKids (the clinical Danish Registry of Childhood and Adolescent Diabetes); children linked to parents through the population registry at Statistics Denmark

definition.value: Interaction of an indicator for the parent's child being diagnosed with type 1 diabetes (treatment group, drawn from DanDiabKids with the exact date of diagnosis recorded) with an indicator for the period at or after the date of diagnosis. Each T1D child is matched to five control children on exact date of birth and sex; control children are assigned a pseudo date of diagnosis equal to the actual diagnosis date of the T1D child they match.

timing.value: post = years at or after the (pseudo-)date of diagnosis; the panel runs from five years before onset (t = -5) to ten years after (t = +10)

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark registry data on parental labor income

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if the parent has positive yearly wage income (labor force participation)

timing.value: measured yearly over the panel, five years before to ten years after the (pseudo-)date of diagnosis

units.value: change in the probability of positive wage income (0/1 outcome; 0.01 = 1 percentage point)

estimand.target_population: Mothers of Danish children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes between 1990 and 2017
estimand.time_horizon: average effect over the post-diagnosis years in the panel, from the year of diagnosis (t = 0) through ten years after
estimand.formal_query: E[Y|do(T1D diagnosis=1)] - E[Y|do(T1D diagnosis=0)] for parents of diagnosed children

population.description: Mothers of children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in Denmark 1990-2017 and mothers of their matched control children, in a yearly panel from five years before to ten years after the (pseudo-)date of diagnosis
population.selection: Children with T1D drawn from the DanDiabKids clinical register; each matched to five control children on exact date of birth and sex; parents linked to children through the population registry at Statistics Denmark

identification.source_of_variation: The onset of type 1 diabetes in a child, which the authors argue is unpredictable, of unknown cause, unrelated to lifestyle and of low inheritability, compared against matched control children's pseudo-onset

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the child's T1D diagnosis, treated and matched control parents would have followed the same path of labor market outcomes
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figs. 1 and 2 show the same level and trend in log wage income for treatment and control parents from five to one year before diagnosis; the event-study estimates in Figs. 3-6 are small and insignificant in the pre-onset years. The authors note this 'does not, however, prove' the counterfactual.

key_assumptions.assumption: The unknown cause(s) of T1D are not related to parental labor market outcomes, i.e. no unobserved common cause of a child's T1D onset and the parent's outcome
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 balance test (for mothers the joint F-test is insignificant, p = 0.24, once immigrant status is excluded); the medical evidence that T1D inheritability is low and the cause unknown and unrelated to lifestyle

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: parents do not adjust the outcome before the child's diagnosis
key_assumptions.supported_by: The onset is described as rapid and unpredictable; Thingholm et al. (2020) find school absenteeism of children who will be diagnosed diverges only four months before diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: The control group is not contaminated with children who have T1D but are undiagnosed, because untreated T1D is fatal
key_assumptions.supported_by: Medical background on T1D (Hakim et al., 2010)

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis sample is conditioned on the matched design: each T1D child is matched to five control children on exact date of birth and sex, and controls are assigned a pseudo date of diagnosis
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction described in Section 3

implies_edges.from: Child's exact date of birth and sex
implies_edges.to: Inclusion in the matched estimation sample

threats_discussed: The unknown cause(s) of T1D could themselves be related to parental labor market outcomes
Treatment and control parents are not balanced on immigrant status (and, for fathers, on other characteristics)
Treatment and control parents differ slightly in number of children and academic education
robustness_checks: Difference-in-differences estimated with and without individual fixed effects
Difference-in-differences re-estimated leaving out the year of diagnosis
Event-study specification showing pre-onset differences are small and insignificant
Balance test of parental characteristics on the probability of a T1D diagnosis within two years (Table 2)
Heterogeneity by maternal immigrant status, the one characteristic that does not balance (Table 4, Panel E)
Model estimated with a diabetes group indicator instead of individual fixed effects (very similar results)
Separate regressions across maternal sub-samples instead of interaction terms (described as extremely similar)
unresolved_confounders: Some unobservable factor correlated with both T1D onset and parental labor supply

estimation.specification: Eq. (2): matched-group (birth year by sex) and year fixed effects, no individual fixed effects; year of diagnosis included

definition.value: Interaction of an indicator for the parent's child being diagnosed with type 1 diabetes (treatment group, drawn from DanDiabKids with the exact date of diagnosis recorded) with an indicator for the period at or after the date of diagnosis. key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the child's T1D diagnosis, treated and matched control parents would have followed the same path of labor market outcomes
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figs. 1 and 2 show the same level and trend in log wage income for treatment and control parents from five to one year before diagnosis; the event-study estimates in Figs. 3-6 are small and insignificant in the pre-onset years. The authors note this 'does not, however, prove' the counterfactual.

key_assumptions.assumption: The unknown cause(s) of T1D are not related to parental labor market outcomes, i.e. no unobserved common cause of a child's T1D onset and the parent's outcome
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 balance test (for mothers the joint F-test is insignificant, p = 0.24, once immigrant status is excluded); the medical evidence that T1D inheritability is low and the cause unknown and unrelated to lifestyle

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: parents do not adjust the outcome before the child's diagnosis
key_assumptions.supported_by: The onset is described as rapid and unpredictable; Thingholm et al. (2020) find school absenteeism of children who will be diagnosed diverges only four months before diagnosis

key_assumptions.assumption: The control group is not contaminated with children who have T1D but are undiagnosed, because untreated T1D is fatal
key_assumptions.supported_by: Medical background on T1D (Hakim et al., 2010)
